query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. cited_evidence.kind: web:Characteristics of NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV HEAs
cited_evidence.text: Alloys of nominal compositions of NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV were synthesized, and in situ neutron-diffraction (ND) measurements were performed (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2, and Supplementary Fig. 1). The ND patterns show a single BCC solid solution at all temperatures up to 1,173 K (Figs. 2a and 3a). Atom probe tomography reveals NbTaTiV to contain 1.15 at.% (atomic percent) O and 0.45 at.% N, while CrMoNbV has low interstitial contents (0.083 at.% O, 0.034 at.% N, and 0.062 at.% C). The CrMoNbV also has an attractive density (ρ = 8.08 g/cm3) with a melting point of Tm ~ 2502 K and is studied in the as-cast state. Figure 1 shows the measured yield strengths (σy) versus temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; high strength is retained up to 1173 K (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). The strength of NbTaTiV is comparable to MoNbTaW and MoNbTaWV, which have been novel among BCC HEAs for their exceptional high-T strength retention, and have been predicted to be controlled by edge dislocations. Moreover, the CrMoNbV alloy has the highest reported strength at the homologous temperature of 1173 K.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a great deal of attention in recent years due to their excellent mechanical properties, such as good ductility, superior fatigue properties, and high strength, thermal stability, and wear resistance. The name refers to the new design philosophy of alloying by introducing more metal elements. The most well-known HEA is the equimolar ratio CoCrFeNiMn alloy, also known as the Cantor alloy,. Although it has a complicated chemical composition, it forms a simple solid solution phase that gives it extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness at elevated temperatures (approximately 900 °C). The yield strength and tensile strength of CoCrFeNiMn, however, is relatively low, and this imbalanced mechanical performance limits its potential applications. Therefore, it is crucial to improve its strength without introducing additional brittleness. The strength of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy is affected by the phase of its microstructures.
